title: Struck Once, Heard All Morning
logline: A bell is struck once at first light on a rock temple standing above a narrow valley, and the film stays with that single impact all the way out: across the roofs, off the far cliff, down to the last second anyone can hear, and then through a morning that has been arranged around it. The same rock is where a body of text carried in living memory was deliberately cut into palm leaf, because memory had been judged unsafe — so the film performs the small version of that decision in one second, and says the large one out loud over the valley the sound crosses.
human_question: How much of what is in your mind right now is what is in front of you, and how much is the fading of something that already finished — and what would you do if you decided the fading could not be trusted?

place.what_kind_of_place: A working rock temple built into a jumble of granite outcrops on a hillside above a narrow inland valley: a dozen or so caves under overhangs, each with a groove cut along the brow of the rock above its mouth so the rain drips clear, short letters in a very early script cut under some of those grooves, whitewashed shrine fronts, stairways built and cut between boulders, a stupa on the highest ledge, and a room at the end of a terrace where leaf books are kept. Monks and lay helpers keep the place and its hours. The film stays outside: it does not enter the shrines or the leaf room, and nothing is opened or brought out for it. Below and around it the valley runs north and south, with a main road, a scatter of tiled roofs, home gardens, spice plots and paddy, and the far side rising into rock and forest.
place.why_it_is_worth_watching: Because it produces one shot that is also one idea, and because the same rock holds the same idea at a scale a thousand times larger. The bell hangs where the rock ends and the valley begins, so a camera can hold the bronze, the hand, the drop and the whole inhabited valley in the same frame, and then leave with the sound. Everything the film needs after that is already there and repeats daily: a single measurable impact, a landscape wide enough to let it travel, a cliff opposite to return part of it, and a morning that goes on long after the sound has gone. And the caves behind the bell are where a recitation was once turned into marks on leaves, and where the marks later burned, which is the same event-and-aftermath shape stretched across two thousand years instead of forty seconds.
place.what_moves_or_changes: The sound, which is the only thing in the film that is doing anything, and which is different every day: still air carries it to the far side of the valley, wind takes it away, mist holds it close, rain erases it. The light, which comes up the valley and arrives at the rock before it reaches the houses, and which finds the cut grooves and the early letters under them at a very low angle for a few minutes only. And the hours of the place, which are fixed and older than anyone keeping them, so that the strike is not an event that has to be arranged for.
place.when_it_looks_best: The last twenty minutes before sunrise and the first ten after it, on a still, clear, windless morning at the end of the dry season, when the valley is quiet enough that a bell carries and mist is lying low enough to show where the sound is going.

two_layers.without_the_philosophy: A sound film with a landscape in it. Dark, then bronze, then one strike, and after that a slow flight out over a waking valley while a single note thins to nothing: birds coming off a tree, a dog, a shutter, a bus, the first smoke. Then the light coming back onto a very old rock, and a whole morning in a place whose day was started by the strike. It works with no commentary at all, and it is the kind of piece people play again for the sound.
two_layers.with_the_philosophy: The same strike becomes the sources' own image. They compare a single sense contact to a bell struck once and left to fade, and say that after the contact has ceased it can go on setting off hundreds or thousands of further movements of mind, pulling related things in with it. The film gives that image its literal form first, so that when the voice turns it inward the viewer already has the measurement: this is how long one strike lasted out there, and this is how much longer it lasted in here. Then the voice raises the scale without changing the subject. Two items on the source's own list of what starts such a movement are hearing what someone says and reading a book — the only two ways a long text has ever been carried — and on this rock, in the first century before our era, a text carried by the first was moved onto the second because the first no longer seemed safe. The rest of the record finishes the argument on its own: the second base burned in 1848, and what replaced it was cut again from recitation and from copies, between 1981 and 1991. One decision, and everything downstream of it that is no longer the decision. The film does not argue that the sources say anything about books. It shows that the distinction they draw was acted on here, once, at civilisational scale.

sequence.on_screen: Dark. The valley below as a shape rather than a place, a few lights. The bell in the foreground, unlit, not moving. Behind it the rock is only a mass. Held long. Insects, a dog a long way off.
sequence.voice: Nothing has happened yet. In about a minute one thing will happen, and it will take less than a second.

sequence.on_screen: The strike, in one shot: the beam swung, the bronze taking it, the shiver in the metal, and the sound going out over the drop.
sequence.voice: There. That is the whole of it. The cause is finished.

sequence.on_screen: The camera leaves the rock and travels out across the valley with the sound: roofs, a road, a river bend, mist in the low ground. Birds coming off a tree line below. A dog. A shutter going up. Flown if a drone is cleared; if not, the same move built on the ground from the terrace edge and a long lens.
sequence.voice: The old manuals use exactly this. A bell struck once, they say, goes on sounding without a second strike; in the same way one contact through one sense, already over, can set off hundreds and even thousands of further movements of mind, drawing other things in as it goes [C048-M:L7-L9].

sequence.on_screen: Animals and objects, not faces: cattle lifting their heads in a yard, a flock turning, a bicycle slowing, a curtain moving. Then the returning sound off the far cliff, a beat late, filmed on the cliff itself.
sequence.voice: The books are careful about that first movement. Something turns the mind toward what has arrived, and that turning cannot recognise anything at all; it only points. It carries nothing good or bad in it and belongs to nobody [C010-P:L29-L37; C010-M:L11-L15]. The hinge is not the person going through the door.

sequence.on_screen: Three fixed positions at increasing distance, cut in sequence, each holding until the note is gone: at the bell, on a roof halfway down, at the bottom of the valley. The last of them ends in ordinary morning noise.
sequence.voice: Out here the fading can be timed. The source's list of what starts this kind of movement is plain and physical: something sensed, what someone said to you, something read, a question put to you, thinking, an upset in the body, hunger, thirst, pain, running into a friend or an enemy [C048-M:L3-L19]. Two of those are the only two ways a long text has ever been carried — hearing what someone says, and reading — and the books set them side by side, as starters of the same kind of process, and add that whatever arrives that way pulls in everything connected to it [C048-M:L11-L13].

sequence.on_screen: The light arriving on the rock itself, which it reaches before the houses: cave mouths under their overhangs, the grooves cut along the brows so the rain drips clear, short early letters under one of them, a whitewashed front, the stupa on the top ledge. Exteriors only. Nothing is opened and nothing is brought out.
sequence.voice: In the first century before our era the monks who had been carrying the three baskets in memory came together and had them written down in books, because a famine and an invasion had made it look as though the teaching might not last. That much is in the chronicles. Where they did it is not: that it was this rock, and that there were five hundred of them, comes from a Sinhala work written some thirteen hundred years afterwards. By that account the version had to be recited and agreed before anything was cut, and the books know that step. A sound arriving is not yet knowing what you heard. That takes further movements of mind — one on the sound now past, one on its name, one on what the name refers to — and the source is honest enough to record it as one teacher's account rather than the only one [C048-M:L23-L27].

sequence.on_screen: Full morning and then the day going: sweeping, water carried, a flower tray, a bus arriving below, a closed door at the end of a terrace that the film does not go through. Late afternoon. Then night: the valley dark again, the lamps, the shape of the rock. The bell in the last of the light, unmoving.
sequence.voice: The books keep three things apart: a thing while it is being sensed, the same thing after it has ceased and is only remembered, and its name, which belongs to no time at all [C047-M:L3-L25; C047-P:L25]. In 1848 British troops attacked this place while putting down a rebellion in the country around it, and the library burned. What is kept here now was cut, leaf by leaf, between 1981 and 1991, and it carries the same name. So did the sound. What was struck this morning ceased this morning; whatever anyone in this valley still has of it is not the sound, but a different event with the same name, happening now [C047-M:L9; C047-M:L11].

sequence.on_screen: The following dawn. The same frame as the opening: bronze, valley, dark. Nothing has been struck yet.
sequence.voice: None of this needed a listener who was separate from the hearing. It needed a bell, some air, and a morning. Nothing on this rock has ever needed more than that — and everything on it that lasted was a copy of something that had already stopped.

concept_merge.why_together: C048 supplies the film's image and its claim in one line, since the source itself reaches for a bell struck once and left to fade in order to say that a single contact, already finished, can set off hundreds or thousands of mind-door processes and draw related things in with them [C048-M:L7-L9], and it supplies the ordinary causes of such movements, from what someone said to hunger and pain [C048-M:L3-L19], along with the further steps by which a person comes to know that they heard something [C048-M:L23-L27]. Two items on that list of causes carry the film's second scale: hearing what others say, and reading books, which the source places side by side as starters of the same kind of process and then says drag in everything connected with what was heard or read [C048-M:L11-L13]. C010 supplies the very first beat of all that: a turning toward which cannot yet recognise anything, carries no good or bad, and is nobody's achievement [C010-P:L29-L37; C010-M:L11-L15]. C047 supplies the wall between the two halves of the film, since a thing heard and a thing remembered are different objects with different lives, a name belongs to no time at all, and remembering a thing is not the same act as remembering that you encountered it [C047-M:L9; C047-M:L11; C047-M:L17; C047-P:L25]. Together they let one strike carry the whole arc from arrival to long afterwards, and they let the rock's own history be said in the same terms without any change of subject.
concept_merge.what_it_reveals: That the difference between what is in front of a mind and what is merely still sounding in it is real, measurable in the first case and invisible in the second, and that the second is most of the day. C048 alone would be a simile. C010 alone is a hinge with nothing on it. C047 alone is a distinction. Put on one bell and one valley, they give a viewer a length they can hold: the sound lasted this long out there, and the film demonstrates without arguing that it lasted very much longer everywhere else. The history then shows the distinction being acted on rather than only described. Somebody on this rock decided that a process which runs with nothing in front of it could not be relied on any longer, and moved a text off it; the thing they moved it onto burned; and the replacement was made again out of recitation and copying. The film does not present that as a lesson about books. It presents it as the same shape at the other end of the scale — one event, and everything downstream of it that is no longer the event — which is exactly what the bell does in forty seconds.

concept_links.why: The digest gives the source's own bell: struck once, fading without a second strike, and used to say that a single sense contact can set off hundreds or thousands of mind-door processes, pulling related objects in with them [C048-M:L7-L9]. It also gives the list of ordinary causes, sense contact and what is connected with it, what others say, reading, a question, thinking, disturbance of the bodily elements, hunger and thirst, bodily pains, and meeting friends or enemies [C048-M:L3-L19], and the account of how the knowledge that one heard something is assembled in further processes, which the source records as one teacher's view [C048-M:L23-L27]. The digest's limits are honoured in the writing. The list is narrated as a list of causes and never as a warning against overthinking, which the digest says adds a judgement the source does not make. The passing mention of spirits supplying objects to the mind [C048-M:L19] is neither presented as fact nor mocked; it is simply not used. Sleep and dreams, which the extract also covers, are left out rather than mixed with sleep science, and no dream in this film is treated as a message or a sign, since the source only calls such impulsions weak [C048-P:L33]. The traditional humoral cause is not translated into hormones or brain chemistry. Two entries in that list of causes carry the film's second scale and are the only part of the history that rests on the digest rather than on the film's own reasoning: hearing what others say, and reading books, which the source names consecutively as starters of the same kind of process and then says pull in everything connected with what was heard or read [C048-M:L11-L13]. That is a narrow and checkable claim and the film keeps it narrow. The digest says nothing about textual transmission, nothing about memory being more or less reliable than writing, and nothing that ranks the two channels; the voice therefore states the history as history and lets the doctrine say only what it says. The digest's own note that the list is explicitly partial is respected, since the film narrates it as a portion rather than as an inventory.

The digest keeps three things strictly apart: a thing while it is being sensed, the same thing remembered once it has ceased, and the name, which belongs to no time at all [C047-M:L3-L25; C047-M:L9; C047-M:L11]. That separation is the difference between the first half of this film, which can be timed with a stopwatch, and the second, which cannot be filmed at all. The digest's note that the mind door is itself a particular mind-moment rather than a figure of speech [C047-P:L25] is respected in the narration. Its limits are carried: the film does not say the past is unreal, since the digest insists that past matter really existed and ceased and is a legitimate object; it adds no judgement about living in the past; it makes no claim that turning toward something distant connects anyone to it; and the digest's note that the source's worked example names a real monument, which is source text and never a location suggestion for this series, is observed, since the location here was chosen for a bell and a valley and takes nothing from the example. Two further lines in the digest earn their place in the finished film. The worked example says that turning from a distance toward a place one remembers takes as its object whatever stands there now rather than the memory [C047-M:L11], and that remembering a thing and remembering that one encountered it are two different acts that the reader is asked not to confuse [C047-M:L17]. Those give the film its late beat without any editorialising: what is kept on this rock now carries the same name as what was there before, and the source's own distinction is enough to say that a name holding across a break is not the same as a thing holding across it. The digest's statement that concepts and the unconditioned come to the mind door free of time [C047-P:L25] is what licenses the line about a name belonging to no time, and the digest's limits are still carried: the past is not called unreal, no judgement is added about living in the past, and the burning of a library is not narrated as a loss of something that was still there to lose.

The digest describes the two adverting minds as the turning toward that everybody does hundreds of times an hour: a sound arrives and the mind swings to it before it has any idea what it is, and the source is precise that this moment cannot recognise anything and carries nothing good or bad of its own [C010-P:L29-L37; C010-M:L11-L15]. That is the fourth beat of this film, filmed on animals and objects rather than on anyone's face. The digest's limits are decisive here and are all kept. Adverting is not presented as mindfulness or presence, because it happens in everyone automatically with no quality of care attached. The arahant's quiet smile [C010-P:L41; C010-M:L19] is not used at all, and nobody in this temple is framed as having it, since that would be a claim about a real person's attainment. The classical grades of laughter and their link to undeveloped character [C010-M:L25] are not used to read anyone. And the traditional placement of the mind door in the heart cavity [C010-M:L11] is not asked of the audience as a literal fact.

what_the_viewer_could_understand: That a single short event can occupy a mind for very much longer than it occupied the air, and that the two are not the same thing. After this film the difference between hearing a bell and going on hearing it is not an idea; it is something the viewer has just been made to sit through. And that the distinction is not a private curiosity: it was once acted on here at full scale, by people who decided that something held only in mind was no longer safe to hold that way, and the record of what happened next makes the same point twice more without anyone having to draw it out.
what_must_be_real: The hour, the strike and the people whose place this is. The bell is struck when it is struck, once, as part of the temple's own morning; it is not struck again for a better angle, not struck early, and not struck for the camera at all. Recording levels and positions are arranged around the temple's routine rather than the reverse. Nobody in or below the temple is presented as the one who hears, and no face is used to supply a listener the concepts deny; the turning belongs to the valley. No monk or keeper is presented as devout, learned, composed or attained, and nobody appears who could not meaningfully refuse the camera. Devotion is not treated as decoration; no act of worship is interrupted, restarted or lit for filming; the film does not enter shrine spaces or the leaf room without permission and does not film anyone at prayer who has not agreed to it. No manuscript is handled, opened or displayed for the camera unless those responsible freely offer it, and the film is built so that it works entirely if they never do: the history is carried by the voice over rock, air and valley. The 1848 sentence is said once, in the words the record supports, with no adjudication and no pathos, and the rewriting between 1981 and 1991 is stated as a fact and not as a recovery.
position_hint: Middle to late: it comes after the films about what arrives at the senses and about processes with visible stages, and it closes the stretch of the group concerned with what a mind keeps doing once the senses have finished. One scheduling constraint now applies across groups rather than within this one. This film names a palm-leaf text and a fire, and IDEA-0005 on another rock monastery turns on a palm-leaf commentary; the two must not sit near each other in any running order, and should be watched back to back once to confirm they have stayed different films.
risks: Turning a working temple's morning into a set. The strike belongs to the place's day, and any request to repeat it would destroy the film's only real subject.
Framing a monk, a keeper or a villager as the one who hears, which is precisely the thing the group's concepts deny.
Letting the adverting moment be dressed up as mindfulness or presence. The C010 digest is explicit that it happens automatically in everyone with no quality of care attached.
Any suggestion that a person on screen has the quiet smile the sources reserve for a fully liberated person, or any reading of people by how they laugh [C010-M:L19; C010-M:L25].
Adding the judgement that dwelling on things is unhealthy. The C048 digest says the source's list of causes is descriptive and makes no such claim.
Bringing dreams in as messages or signs, or setting the source's claims about sleep beside sleep science as though they agreed.
Translating the traditional humoral cause of mental disturbance into modern claims about hormones or brain chemistry.
A sound track rebuilt in post. If the decay is sweetened, extended or layered, the film's one measurable fact has been falsified.

Letting the 1848 line become a wound. The record says troops attacked the place while a rebellion was being put down and the library burned. That is stated once and flat, never adjudicated, never made into a crime, a tragedy or anyone's grievance or anyone's due, and C061's bar on legacy and remembrance framing is live: this is not a film about what was lost.

Letting the rewriting between 1981 and 1991 read as a recovery, a restoration or a vindication. It is a further event with its own causes. The concepts give no warrant for an arc, and an arc is exactly what would make the film sentimental.

Overstating the history. The chronicles give two sentences, no place, no number, no leader and no duration; 'the place where the canon was first written down' is not a claim the chronicles make in that form and most scholars doubt it in that form. The voice says what the chronicles say and then says where the rest comes from.

Implying that this series' own books were written here. The chronicles say the three baskets and their commentary, which includes the Abhidhamma basket; the compendium and the Sinhala expositions this series actually reads are many centuries later and no source connects them to this rock. The voice must not let the two touch.
Drifting into a manuscript film. The moment a leaf is held up to the lens this becomes IDEA-0005's neighbour rather than its opposite, and the slate already has that film.
Naming the place in the voice. A king, a chronicle, a rebellion and a colonial power may be named; the temple, the town, the district and the valley may not.
drop_if: There is no single dawn strike at the site, or the bell is rung as a peal, which would remove the film's premise.
The temple does not want a camera present at its morning, or the shrine and leaf spaces cannot be approached with consent.
It could only be made by asking for the bell to be struck for the camera.
The history can only be included by filming manuscripts. If nothing may be shown but leaves, the second scale is dropped and the film reverts to the bell alone rather than becoming a manuscript film.
The 1848 record cannot be stated on the terms above — that is, if the only available way to include it is to adjudicate it, or if the rewriting can only be narrated as a recovery.

connections.note: One film stays at the moment of arrival and shows what is added to it; this one starts after the arrival is over and follows what is left.
The same turning-toward in two settings: one where it happens hundreds of times an hour among people, and one where a whole valley does it at once, to a sound, before anyone knows what it is.

Both films stand on a rock monastery whose history involves palm leaves, which is close enough to be a real risk, so the separation is stated rather than assumed. That film is about a commentary that made an illegible chronicle readable: its subject is legibility, its material is manuscripts, lamplight and cave interiors in monsoon, and it is the wettest, most nearly droneless film on the slate. This one is about a recitation being externalised and then burned: its subject is one event and everything downstream of it that is no longer the event, its material is bronze, air, a valley and low light on outside rock at dawn, and it films no manuscript at all. Nothing is handled, opened, read or displayed here; the history is carried in the voice over landscape, and the film is built to work if nothing is ever brought out. If the two ever start to look like one film, this is the one that gives up the leaves, because its spine is a sound.

selection.reason: It is the source's own image standing in a real landscape, and it gives a viewer a measured length for something the sources say cannot be watched.

review.note: Revised 2026-09-26 to add a full historical_thread and to integrate that history into the film. The research established that the Dipavamsa and Mahavamsa record, in two sentences, that in the reign of Vattagamani Abhaya monks who had carried the three pitakas and the atthakatha orally came together and wrote them down in books, and that neither chronicle names a place, a number of monks, a leader or a duration; that the identification of this rock as the cave of light, and the figure of five hundred monks, come from the thirteenth-century Pujavaliya and the eighteenth-century Asgiri Talpata, some thirteen hundred years and more after the event; that the date is genuinely unsettled between Geiger's 1912 chronology and later Sinhalese chronologies; that no manuscript from that writing-down survives anywhere; that every account of the site records British troops attacking the temple in 1848 while a rebellion in the country around it was being suppressed and the library burning, while the general histories of that rebellion reachable here do not mention it and one scholarly site summary generalises instead to repeated colonial damage across the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries; and that the 1982 date for the first basket sits inside a documented rewriting on talipot leaf at the temple between 1981 and 1991 by a small number of trained writers, some of them lay. All of that is in the thread, with certainty and dispute kept apart. On integration: the bell stays the spine and the history enters in two beats, and that was a decision rather than a default. C048's own figure IS a bell struck once and left to fade, so making the manuscripts the spine would throw away the one place where the source hands this film its image; the bell is also the only thing here that gives a viewer a measurable length, which the history cannot; and a manuscript-spine film would have to be shot on leaves being handled, which the floor makes conditional at a living temple and which would collide head-on with IDEA-0005. What the history does instead is raise the scale without changing the subject, because it is the same shape — one event, and everything downstream of it that is no longer the event. The bridge is argued rather than asserted and rests on one narrow, checkable point: hearing what others say and reading books are two consecutive items on C048's own list of what starts a mind-door process [C048-M:L11-L13], and they are the only two ways a long text has ever been carried. Everything past that is named in how_it_binds as the film's own reasoning, since C048 and C047 are about causes and occasions and say nothing about textual transmission. Beat 6 is new and carries the writing-down together with its own dispute, and reuses the follow-on processes by which a heard sound becomes knowledge of what was heard [C048-M:L23-L27] against the traditional account that the version had to be recited and agreed before it was cut. Beat 7 absorbs 1848 and the 1981-1991 rewriting into the existing C047 beat, stated once and flat, with the doctrinal weight carried by the distinction between a thing sensed, a thing remembered and a name outside time [C047-M:L3-L25; C047-P:L25] and the closing line about a different event with the same name [C047-M:L9; C047-M:L11] — which now does the whole second act without editorialising. No beat is exposition: both history beats are on footage the film was already shooting. The old beat that used C048-M:L23-L27 over the full morning was folded into beat 6, and the old two-C047 arrangement became one denser C047 beat, so the count stays at eight. logline, human_question, place, two_layers, concept_merge, what_the_viewer_could_understand, what_must_be_real, position_hint, risks, drop_if, connections and unknowns were all revised; the C048 and C047 links were extended rather than rewritten, so their existing citations are untouched. New citations are C048-M:L11-L13, C047-M:L17 and C047-P:L25, each read in the source before use. The title is unchanged because the spine is unchanged. Three constraints were held deliberately. First, an explicit connections entry now separates this from IDEA-0005 and commits this film to giving up the leaves if the two ever converge; no manuscript is handled, read or displayed, and the film is built to work if nothing is ever offered. Second, 1848 is recorded and never adjudicated: no wound, no crime, no grievance, no legacy framing, and the rewriting is denied any redemptive arc. Third, no claim is made that this series' own sources were written here — the chronicles say the three baskets and the commentary, which includes the Abhidhamma basket, and the risks now state plainly that the later compendium and its Sinhala expositions have no recorded connection to this rock. Drone remains uncertain over a protected monument and a ground fallback for the travelling shot is now written into the beat, what_to_film and access, so the film no longer drops on a refused flight. Because the body has been rewritten rather than only researched, the verdict stays pending.

suggested_location.name: Aluvihare Rock Temple and the valley below it, north of Matale

also_known_as.name: Alu Viharaya
also_known_as.meaning: the rock temple in the ash-coloured rocks

also_known_as.name: Matale Aluviharaya
also_known_as.meaning: the same site named by its district town

suggested_location.region: Matale District, Central Province: in the granite outcrops on the west side of the valley on the Matale–Dambulla road, about three kilometres north of Matale town
suggested_location.why_here: It gives the film a bell at the edge of a drop with an inhabited valley under it, which is the whole requirement, and it gives the film a second reason that no other bell would. The temple is a working one built into a dozen or so rock caves in a jumble of outcrops, with drip grooves cut along the cave brows, very early inscriptions under some of them, stairways between boulders, a stupa on an upper ledge and a leaf-book room, and it stands high enough above the valley floor for a camera to leave the rock and travel out with a sound over roofs, road and gardens to rock and forest on the far side. Its hours are its own and very old, so the strike the film needs is part of the day rather than an event to be arranged. And by a tradition recorded from the thirteenth century onward this is the place where a body of text carried in memory was deliberately converted into marks on palm leaf because memory was judged unsafe; where the marks burned in 1848; and where they were cut again between 1981 and 1991. That is the film's own subject at a scale the bell cannot reach, on the same rock as the bell.

historical_thread.story:
The event itself is recorded twice, very briefly. Both the Dipavamsa, the older chronicle of about the fourth century CE, and the Mahavamsa, compiled in the fifth or sixth, state that in the reign of Vattagamani Abhaya — Valagamba in Sinhala usage — the monks who had until then carried the three pitakas and the atthakatha orally came together and had them written down in books. Geiger's standard English translation of the Mahavamsa passage reads: 'The text of the three pitakas and the atthakatha thereon did the most wise bhikkhus hand down in former times orally, but since they saw that the people were falling away (from religion) the bhikkhus came together, and in order that the true doctrine might endure, they wrote them down in books.' That is the whole of it in the chronicle. No place is named. No number of monks is given. No leader is named, and no duration.

The chronicles do supply the circumstances. Valagamba lost Anuradhapura to a South Indian force, spent fourteen or fifteen years in exile in the hill country, and returned to take the capital back. Across those years the island suffered the twelve-year famine remembered as the Beminitiya Seya, the famine of the brahmin Tiya. The monastic community scattered; later accounts say some sixty bhikkhus went into the Malaya, the hill country, and lived there until conditions eased. The reason the chronicle gives for the writing-down is not that memory fails but that the people were falling away and the doctrine might not endure.

Everything specific about the place belongs to a much later layer of the record. The identification of the site as Aloka-lena or Alu-lena, the cave of light, in the Matula district — Matale — appears in the Pujavaliya, the Sinhala work of Mayurapada Buddhaputra Thera of the thirteenth century, and again in the eighteenth-century Asgiri Talpata. The figure of five hundred scholarly monks, reciting the doctrine and agreeing an acceptable version before it was transcribed, belongs to that same late Sinhala tradition and to the modern retellings that follow it. Those retellings add further detail that the chronicles do not carry: that the work was led by a Maharakkhita Thera in some versions and by a Kuntagatta or Kunthagattha Tissa Thera in others; that the patron was the ruler of Matula rather than the king himself in some accounts and the king in others; that it took more than three years, or three years, three months and three weeks; that it was finished on a Vesak full-moon day; and that copies were deposited at this site and at Abhayagiri. Popular Sri Lankan accounts frequently attribute these details to the Mahavamsa, which does not contain them. The site is also widely described in the Buddhist world as the venue of the Fourth Buddhist Council, though some accounts number it the Fifth. The books were puskola poth: strips cut from palmyra or talipot palm, boiled, dried and oiled, and written with a metal stylus.

What is on the ground is older than the tradition that explains it. The temple occupies a landslip of granite with thirteen caves identified under overhangs, each with a drip ledge cut along the brow of the rock so rain runs clear of the cave mouth. Early Brahmi inscriptions of roughly the third century BC to the first century AD are cut under several of those ledges; Paranavitana's Inscriptions of Ceylon includes one that reads as the cave of the lay devotee Sumana and of the elder Deva. Devanampiya Tissa is credited locally with the dagoba and a bo sapling in the third century BC. The caves now hold much later plaster and painting: Jataka scenes, a reclining figure, a cave given over to the punishments of hell, a cave dedicated to Buddhaghosa, who is said by tradition to have worked here in the fifth century, and a cave shown as the Sangayana Lena with modern figures of monks writing on talipot leaf. An international Buddhist library was begun at the site in 1956 and completed by 1974. The drip-ledged caves and the caves with inscriptions were declared archaeological protected monuments by gazette notification of 11 October 1974.

The second act is 1848. The hill-country rebellion broke out at the end of July that year; Lord Torrington declared martial law on 29 July. Accounts of the site, including the temple's own, the Central Province tourism department's and the standard guide and gazetteer entries, record that British troops attacked the temple in the course of putting the rebellion down and that the library burned, with many of the manuscripts kept there lost. How much was destroyed is described differently in different places. Separately, no manuscript from the first-century-BC writing-down survives, here or anywhere: apart from quotations in inscriptions and a two-page fragment of the eighth or ninth century found in Nepal, the oldest known Pali manuscripts are of the late fifteenth century.

What followed is usually told as a recompilation by hand over a very long time, with the first of the three baskets of the law not finished until 1982. The documented project behind that date is a rewriting of the Tipitaka on talipot leaf carried out at the temple between 1981 and 1991, coordinated by the chief incumbent, Ven. Ethipola Medhankara Nayaka Thera, and executed by a small number of people trained in leaf writing, at least one of them an ayurvedic physician and several of them lay. Those volumes are what the library holds. A Sangayana Perahera, revived in 1973, marks the completion of the original transcription annually. In January 2019 the Tripitaka was declared a national heritage at the temple, with a stated intention of pursuing UNESCO recognition.
historical_thread.how_it_binds:
C048 asks what starts a mind-door process: a run of mind with no physical object in front of it. Its answer is a list, and the list is deliberately ordinary — something sensed and things connected with it, what others say, reading books, a question put to you, thinking, an upset in the bodily elements, hunger and thirst, bodily pains, meeting an enemy or a friend [C048-M:L5-L19]. Two consecutive items on that list are the only two ways a long text has ever been carried anywhere: hearing what someone says, and reading. The source puts them beside each other as starters of the same kind of process, and then adds that whatever arrives by either route drags in everything connected with it [C048-M:L11-L13]. That is the whole of what the digest gives this film, and it is enough, because what is recorded on this rock is a body of text carried by the first of those two channels being deliberately moved onto the second, on the ground that the first could no longer be relied on to keep it.

The limit has to be stated, because the temptation to overclaim here is large. C048 is about causes; C047 is about occasions. Neither says anything about textual transmission, neither ranks memory against writing, and neither would endorse the sentence 'memory is unreliable'. The chronicle's own stated reason is not cognitive at all: the people were falling away and the doctrine might not endure. So the film does not argue that the Abhidhamma predicted or justified what happened here. It argues something narrower and checkable: that a recitation is a mind-door process and a reading is a mind-door process, that the source names both, and that at this place a civilisation moved a text from one to the other and then had to watch what happened to the second. The rest of the connection is the film's own reasoning and is narrated as such, in the chronicles' own hedged terms.

C047 then finishes the argument without help. Its worked example keeps three things strictly apart: a thing while it is being sensed, the same thing after it has ceased and is only remembered, and its name, which is a concept and comes to the mind door free of time altogether [C047-M:L3-L25; C047-P:L25]. It insists that if you turn from a distance toward a place you remember, what you are facing is whatever stands there now and not your memory of it [C047-M:L11], and that remembering a thing and remembering that you encountered it are two different acts [C047-M:L17]. That is exactly the shape of what the record does next. The external base was not safe either; it burned. What is on the shelves now was cut between 1981 and 1991 out of recitation and out of copies, and it carries the same name. A name holding across a break is not a thing holding across it. And the digest's own limits keep the film honest in both directions: past matter is treated as something that really existed and ceased, a legitimate object of mind rather than an illusion, so the fire is not narrated as a wound, and the rewriting is not narrated as a recovery. They are further events, each with its own causes, downstream of a decision that had already finished.

That is why the bell keeps the spine. The film's method is to follow one strike to its last audible second and then through a morning arranged around it: one event, and everything downstream of it that is no longer the event. The history is the same shape at a scale a thousand times larger, and each half gives the other what it lacks. The bell gives the viewer a length they can time, which nothing in the history can supply. The history gives the film the demonstration that the distinction is not a private curiosity — somebody stood on this rock and acted on it.
historical_thread.what_is_certain: That the Dipavamsa and the Mahavamsa both record that in the reign of Vattagamani Abhaya the monks who had carried the three pitakas and the atthakatha orally came together and wrote them down in books, and that the reason the Mahavamsa gives is that the people were falling away and the true doctrine might endure; and that the wording quoted in the story above is Geiger's standard English translation. That neither chronicle names a place, a number of monks, a leader or a duration for this, and that the chronicle passage is two sentences long. That the chronicles' phrase is the three pitakas and the atthakatha, which includes the Abhidhamma pitaka; and that the compendium and the Sinhala expositions this series actually reads are works of many centuries later, connected to this event by no source at all. That the Pujavaliya, the Sinhala work of Mayurapada Buddhaputra Thera of the thirteenth century, and the eighteenth-century Asgiri Talpata do name the venue as Aloka-lena or Alu-lena in the Matula district, and that the figure of five hundred monks belongs to that later Sinhala layer and to modern retellings of it. That the chronicles record a twelve-year famine in this period, remembered as the Beminitiya Seya, and Valagamba's exile of some fourteen or fifteen years followed by his recovery of Anuradhapura. That the site has thirteen identified caves under overhangs in a granite landslip, each with a drip ledge cut along the brow, and Early Brahmi inscriptions of roughly the third century BC to the first century AD cut under several of them, one of which Paranavitana's Inscriptions of Ceylon reads as the cave of the lay devotee Sumana and of the elder Deva. That the drip-ledged caves and the caves with inscriptions were declared archaeological protected monuments by gazette notification of 11 October 1974. That the hill-country rebellion broke out at the end of July 1848 and that Lord Torrington declared martial law on 29 July 1848. That every account of the site that treats the nineteenth century — the temple's own, the provincial tourism department's, the standard guide and gazetteer entries — states that British troops attacked the temple in 1848 while the rebellion was being put down and that the library burned with the loss of many manuscripts. That no manuscript from the first-century-BC writing-down survives here or anywhere, and that apart from inscriptional quotations and a two-page fragment of the eighth or ninth century found in Nepal the oldest known Pali manuscripts are of the late fifteenth century. That a rewriting of the Tipitaka on talipot leaf was carried out at the temple between 1981 and 1991 under the chief incumbent, Ven. Ethipola Medhankara Nayaka Thera, and that the first of the three baskets is given as completed in 1982. That an international Buddhist library was begun at the site in 1956 and completed by 1974, and that in January 2019 the Tripitaka was declared a national heritage in a ceremony at the temple. That the books in question were puskola poth, strips of palmyra or talipot palm inscribed with a metal stylus.
historical_thread.what_is_disputed:
The date, and not marginally. The chronology that puts Vattagamani's second reign at 29-17 BC was devised by Wilhelm Geiger in the preface to his 1912 Mahavamsa translation and does not agree with the datings later researchers into Sinhalese history calculated, which place a first reign at about 103 BC and the second at about 89-77 BC. The writing-down is accordingly dated 29 BC in some places, 35-32 BC in others, and simply 'the first century BC' in most. Nothing settles it.

Whether it happened here at all. The chronicles are silent on the place; the identification with this rock first appears in the thirteenth century, some thirteen hundred years after the event, and is repeated from there. The site's own antiquity is not in question — the inscriptions establish occupation in the right period — but antiquity in the right period is not the same as being the venue.

The five hundred monks. The figure is not in either chronicle. It enters with the late Sinhala works and should be read as the tradition's number for a recital rather than as a count: five hundred is the same figure the tradition uses for the arahants at the first recital at Rajagaha, and formulaic numbers of this kind travel. Nothing found supports it as a head count, and nothing contradicts it either.

Who led it, who paid for it and how long it took. Maharakkhita in some retellings, a Kuntagatta or Kunthagattha Tissa in others; the king in some accounts, the ruler of Matula in others; more than three years, or three years three months and three weeks, finished on a Vesak poya. None of it is in the chronicles, and several Sri Lankan press accounts attribute these details and even a description of the caves being decorated to the Mahavamsa, which does not contain them. The council's number is itself unsettled — Fourth in most accounts, Fifth in some.

Whether 'first written down' is right in the form it is usually given. The chronicle says the monks wrote the texts down in books at that time; it does not say that this was the first use of writing for Buddhist texts anywhere, and most scholars are sceptical that the canon existed then in the form it now has. Steven Collins's remark that the importance of the canon lies in the idea of it rather than in its contents is directly relevant to how much weight the claim can carry. The claim is genuinely held, widely repeated and central to the site's identity; it is also a claim about which the surviving evidence is silent, since nothing written down in that century survives.

The 1848 destruction: its extent, its agents and its documentation. The extent is given variously as the library totally destroyed, largely destroyed, or some manuscripts burned. The agents are given as British troops, and in at least one account as British and Ceylonese Burgher troops; the Ceylon Rifle Regiment was in action in that rebellion but no source found puts it at this temple. More importantly, no contemporary document of 1848-1850 naming this temple was located in this research: the general histories of the rebellion reachable here, including the standard encyclopaedia account, do not mention the library at all, and one careful site gazetteer generalises instead to the temple having been 'vandalised several times by colonial invaders' across the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries, with patronage improving after 1896. The 1848 attribution is therefore firmly established in the site's own literature and in every guide that follows it, and thinly sourced in the general record as it can be reached from a desk. One account adds that the British government later restored the temple; that was not independently confirmed.

The recompilation. One telling has several generations of monks transcribing across more than a century, with the first basket not finished until 1982. The documented project is a single ten-year effort from 1981, with a handful of trained writers, at least one an ayurvedic physician and several of them laymen rather than monks, and the 1982 date for the first basket sits inside it. The two versions are not compatible as they stand, and the more heroic one is the one usually printed.

Smaller points. The protection date is given as 11 October 1974 by gazette and as 1971 on at least one site. Whether Buddhaghosa worked here in the fifth century is traditional and undocumented. Whether Devanampiya Tissa founded the temple in the third century BC is local tradition rather than chronicle.
sources: Bowden, R. (2009). 'Writing down of the Pali Tripitaka at Aloka Vihara in Sri Lanka', Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society of Sri Lanka 55, pp. 115-167 — cited by the Lankapradeepa entry; not read directly and should be obtained before anything in the thread is treated as settled.
Paranavitana, S. (1970). Inscriptions of Ceylon, Vol. I — source of the cave inscription reading, via the Lankapradeepa entry.
Nicholas, C. W. (1963). Historical topography of ancient and medieval Ceylon — cited by the Lankapradeepa entry for the site's identification.
Geiger, W. (1912). The Mahavamsa, or The Great Chronicle of Ceylon — the translation quoted, and the source of the 29-17 BC chronology.
Government of Sri Lanka, Gazette Notification No. 133 of 11 October 1974 — the protected-monument declaration, cited by the Lankapradeepa entry.

what_to_film: The bell and the drop in one frame, in the dark, before anything happens, held long enough for the silence to be the subject.
The strike itself in a single unbroken shot: the swing, the bronze, the shiver in the metal, the sound leaving.

One continuous travelling shot out over the valley with the sound, from the rock to the far side. Drone if it is cleared; if not, the same figure assembled on the ground, from a move along the terrace edge into a long-lens series down the valley and a tracking shot on the road below, cut on the sound rather than on the geography.
The valley answering: birds off a tree line, cattle, a dog, a shutter, a bicycle, filmed on animals and objects rather than faces.
The return of the sound off the far rock face, recorded on the far side.
Three fixed sound positions at increasing distance, each held until the note is completely gone.

The rock itself as the light reaches it, from outside only: cave mouths under their overhangs, the drip grooves cut along the brows, the short early letters under one of them, a whitewashed front, the stupa on the top ledge.
The ordinary morning that follows at the temple: sweeping, water, flowers, the first bus below, and the closed door of the leaf room filmed from the terrace without going in.
The bell in the middle of the day and at dusk, still and ignored.
Nothing inside the leaf room and no manuscript at any point, unless those responsible freely offer it — and the cut is built so that the absence is invisible.
suggested_location.access: By road from the district town on the Dambulla road, then steps and built stairways between the outcrops. This is a functioning temple and an Archaeological Protected Monument, so everything depends on the incumbent monks' agreement and on the Department of Archaeology; a dawn call means being in position the night before. Drone flight is uncertain and should be treated as unlikely rather than merely unconfirmed: the protection notice of 11 October 1974 covers the drip-ledged and inscribed caves specifically, the site is in daily religious use, and permission for flight over a protected monument is granted case by case and is often refused. The ground fallback for the film's one travelling figure is written into what_to_film and is not a compromise: a move along the terrace edge, a long-lens series of fixed positions receding down the valley, and a tracking shot on the road below, cut on the decay of the sound. The film does not drop if the drone is refused.
suggested_location.best_time: The end of the dry season, on a still, clear, windless morning, in the twenty minutes before sunrise and the ten after it. A second morning is needed for the far-side and valley-floor sound positions.

suggested_location.research_note: Desk research only, in two passes: the site and film requirements in September 2026's earlier work, and the historical thread added on 2026-09-26. That the temple is built into thirteen identified rock caves in granite outcrops about three kilometres north of the district town on the Dambulla road, that it holds cave shrines with Jataka murals, drip ledges, Early Brahmi inscriptions and a leaf-book library, and that the drip-ledged and inscribed caves have been protected since the gazette notification of 11 October 1974, are from the sources listed here and in the historical thread. The coordinates are the published position of the temple. The thread was built by going to the chronicle text rather than to the site literature, and that changed the answer: the Mahavamsa passage on the writing-down is two sentences, names no place, no number, no leader and no duration, and the place and the five hundred monks enter the record in the thirteenth century and the eighteenth. Several Sri Lankan press accounts attribute to the Mahavamsa details it does not contain, including the duration and a description of the caves being decorated, which is the same pattern of press versions outliving scholarship that this project has hit before. The 1848 destruction is well attested in the site's own literature and in every guide entry, and thinly sourced in the general record reachable from a desk: no contemporary document of 1848-1850 naming this temple was found, the standard accounts of the rebellion do not mention the library, and the most careful site gazetteer generalises to repeated colonial damage across two centuries instead. That gap is recorded in what_is_disputed rather than smoothed over. Bowden's 2009 Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society of Sri Lanka article on the writing-down at Aloka Vihara was identified but not read, and it is the single most important thing to obtain before any of this is treated as settled. Crucially still unverified on the film side: no source found confirms that a bell is struck once at dawn here, or that there is a bell hung where the rock meets the drop; a morning bell is an ordinary feature of Sri Lankan temple practice but it is an assumption at this site and must be checked before anything else. Also unverified: how open the valley below is and how far a bell actually carries in it, whether the far side gives a usable return, and whether any drone flight is possible over a protected monument — a ground fallback for the travelling shot is now written into what_to_film and access so that the film does not depend on it.

unknowns: Whether a single bell is struck at dawn at this temple at all. Nothing found confirms it, and the film's spine rests on it.
Whether the bell, if there is one, hangs where the rock and the valley can be held in one frame.
How far the sound carries down the valley in still air, and whether the far rock face returns a usable reflection.

Whether the Department of Archaeology and the incumbent monks would permit a dawn crew. Drone flight over a protected monument in daily religious use should be assumed unlikely; the ground fallback is specified and the film does not depend on the flight.
No monk, keeper or household in the valley has been approached. Everything here is a research direction.

Whether any contemporary document of 1848 to 1850 records the attack on this temple and the burning of its library. None was found, and the claim currently rests on the site's own literature and the guide entries that follow it. Bowden's 2009 article in the Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society, listed in the historical thread's sources, is the first thing to obtain.
Which room or building actually burned, where it stood in relation to the present terraces, and whether anything of it is still visible on the ground, as one account asserts.
What, if anything, of the pre-1848 collection survives, and whether the temple's account of its own losses differs from the printed versions.

Whether the temple would want the 1981 to 1991 volumes mentioned at all, and on what terms. Nothing is filmed of them and nothing is asked for; but the voice names them, and that is theirs to accept or refuse.

The dating. Whether the reign is Geiger's 29 to 17 BC or the later 89 to 77 BC changes nothing in the film but everything in any caption, and the voice therefore says 'the first century before our era' and no more.
